heuristics.rule: If 1 in 4 PhD students would change advisors in retrospect, advisor selection is the highest-variance decision in the entire PhD application process — not program rank, not funding type.
heuristics.condition: When choosing between PhD programs where multiple offers are on the table...
heuristics.action: ...weight the specific advisor relationship above program prestige or location, and conduct structured due diligence on the advisor before committing
heuristics.because: 25% advisor regret rate means the prior probability of choosing a bad advisor without deliberate vetting is extremely high

heuristics.rule: Ask a prospective advisor directly: 'How often do you meet one-on-one with PhD students and what does that look like weekly?' — and treat vague answers as a red flag.
heuristics.condition: When evaluating a potential PhD advisor...
heuristics.action: ...demand specifics on meeting cadence and mentoring style, not just research fit
heuristics.because: 50% of PhD students get less than one hour per week with their advisor; access asymmetry is common and predictable, not exceptional

heuristics.rule: Treat institutional mental health resources as a near-zero asset unless independently verified — only 26% of students who used them found them helpful.
heuristics.condition: When a program touts its 'student wellness resources' as a selling point...
heuristics.action: ...discount that claim heavily and instead ask current students whether they have actually used those services and found them useful
heuristics.because: Formal availability of mental health resources does not correlate with actual effectiveness; 2 out of 3 users found institutional support unhelpful

heuristics.rule: High satisfaction scores in PhD surveys do not validate structural conditions — they reflect socialization and sunk-cost commitment, not absence of problems.
heuristics.condition: When a program cites high student satisfaction rates as evidence of program quality...
heuristics.action: ...look past the aggregate satisfaction number and probe specific structural variables: advisor access, bullying rates, career placement, mental health outcomes
heuristics.because: 75% satisfaction coexists with 36% seeking mental health help, 21% being bullied, and 79% reporting career uncertainty — satisfaction is not a proxy for healthy conditions

heuristics.rule: Ask programs for concrete placement data — specifically: what percentage of graduates get faculty positions, what percentage go to industry, and who are recent graduates working for — before accepting any offer.
heuristics.condition: When evaluating career preparation quality of a PhD program...
heuristics.action: ...request actual graduate outcomes data rather than accepting vague statements about career support
heuristics.because: Only 29% of students received useful non-academic career advice from their program, and 60% relied on personal research for career planning — programs systematically overstate career preparation

decision_factors.factor: Advisor meeting frequency and mentoring structure
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Direct access to your advisor determines feedback quality, progress speed, and psychological safety — and 50% of students get under one hour per week, making this highly variable and consequential
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask the advisor directly about typical meeting cadence; ask current and former students in the lab independently to verify; ask how the advisor handled a student who was struggling

decision_factors.factor: Advisor accountability mechanisms in the program
decision_factors.why_it_matters: When supervisors are the primary perpetrators in 48% of bullying cases and over 50% of bullied students feel unable to speak out, the presence or absence of formal oversight structures determines whether abuse can be addressed
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask whether there is a thesis committee with mandatory annual reviews, a formal ombudsperson process, and whether students can change advisors without academic penalty

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Over 50% of PhD students plan academic careers but the academic job market cannot absorb them — programs with no industry placement infrastructure leave students stranded
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask for placement outcomes data by career type for the last five cohorts; ask whether the program has industry partnerships, career workshops, or alumni networks outside academia

decision_factors.factor: Institutional mental health resource quality (not just availability)
decision_factors.why_it_matters: 39% of PhD students score in moderate-to-severe depression range — 6x the general population rate — making mental health support a functional necessity, not a nice-to-have
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask current students whether they have used mental health services and found them useful; ask about wait times and whether counselors have experience with PhD-specific stressors

decision_factors.why_it_matters: ~50% of programs have a long-hours culture; 25% of students work 51-60 hours per week — this directly determines sustainability of the PhD and mental health outcomes
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask current lab members what a typical week looks like; ask whether there are explicit expectations around evenings and weekends; observe whether the advisor emails students on weekends

decision_factors.why_it_matters: 19% of PhD students hold outside jobs, 53% of them out of financial necessity — financial stress compounds mental health and career uncertainty pressures
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Calculate whether the stipend covers actual cost of living in the program city including rent, not just nominal funding adequacy; ask students whether they can live on the stipend without supplementing

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Choosing a high-prestige program with a less accessible advisor
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You inherit the advisor's inaccessibility as a structural feature of your daily experience — brand name provides credential value at graduation but does not protect you from the 50% who get under one hour per week of mentoring
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students who need iterative feedback, come from less elite academic backgrounds, or are working in a new subfield without prior research experience

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Relying on institutional mental health services when struggling
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: 74% of students who use institutional support do not find it helpful — you may experience the delay of seeking help AND the disappointment of it not working, compounding the crisis
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: International students who may already have limited external support networks outside the institution and who may face cultural or visa-related barriers to seeking outside care

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Entering a PhD with the explicit goal of becoming a professor
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Over 50% plan academic careers but only 6% expect to become an assistant professor directly after PhD — the gap between aspiration and outcome is built into the structure, not the individual's failure, but programs rarely communicate this proactively
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students who have not built industry-transferable skills or networks during the PhD, and who discover the career gap only after graduating

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting that high satisfaction rates among current students signal a healthy program
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Satisfaction is contaminated by sunk-cost commitment and socialization into academic culture — students who are bullied, depressed, or career-uncertain still report 75% overall satisfaction, meaning satisfaction scores actively obscure structural problems
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Prospective students conducting due diligence who use student satisfaction surveys as a primary signal of program quality

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Staying silent about bullying or harassment by a supervisor
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Over 50% of bullied students feel unable to speak out — the power asymmetry that makes speaking up risky also ensures the behavior continues and the student absorbs the psychological cost alone
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: International students whose visa status is tied to their enrollment and who have greater material risk attached to confronting or leaving an abusive advisor relationship

failure_patterns.pattern: Selecting an advisor based on research fit alone without vetting mentoring behavior
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Applicants are trained to optimize for intellectual alignment and publication record — advisor interpersonal behavior is harder to assess from the outside and rarely discussed in application advice
failure_patterns.consequence: 1 in 4 PhD students ends up wishing they had chosen a different advisor — the single highest-regret decision in the PhD
warning_signs: Advisor gives vague or evasive answers when asked directly about meeting frequency with students
Current lab members seem reluctant to discuss their advisor candidly or give uniformly positive but generic responses

failure_patterns.pattern: Assuming institutional mental health resources will be adequate when selecting a program
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Programs advertise wellness services in recruitment materials; prospective students have no basis to evaluate quality before enrolling and take availability as a proxy for adequacy
failure_patterns.consequence: Students reach a crisis point, seek institutional help, find it unhelpful, and have no backup plan — delaying recovery and compounding the academic and mental health damage
warning_signs: Program describes mental health resources in marketing language without specifying wait times or PhD-specialist availability
No current students can give a specific account of actually using and benefiting from the service

failure_patterns.pattern: Planning exclusively for an academic career without building industry-exit options
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Academic culture frames industry as a fallback for those who 'couldn't make it' — students internalize this and avoid developing non-academic skills or networks to signal commitment to academia
failure_patterns.consequence: When the academic job market fails them — as it does the majority — they graduate with no industry network, no translated resume, and no relationships with non-academic employers
warning_signs: Student cannot name a single non-academic employer who has hired recent graduates from their program
Student has never attended an industry networking event or informational interview during their PhD

failure_patterns.pattern: Taking a PhD offer without asking about advisor accountability structures
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Applicants focus on research opportunities and funding; questions about what happens if the advisor relationship breaks down feel presumptuous or negative before starting
failure_patterns.consequence: When bullying or mismanagement occurs — which it does to roughly 1 in 10 PhD students via their supervisor — the student has no mapped pathway to address it without jeopardizing their degree
warning_signs: Program has no mandatory thesis committee with independent oversight of student progress
There is no formal process for changing advisors that doesn't require withdrawing from the program

failure_patterns.pattern: Using high overall PhD satisfaction rates as a signal of structural program health
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Satisfaction is the most visible and easily communicated metric; it aligns with what programs want to advertise and what prospective students want to hear
failure_patterns.consequence: Students enroll in programs with serious structural deficits — mental health crises, bullying, career preparation gaps — that were masked by surface-level satisfaction data
warning_signs: Program cites satisfaction survey results but cannot provide data on depression rates, bullying incidence, or career placement by type
All student testimonials in program materials are positive with no discussion of challenges

diagnostic_questions.question: How often does your prospective advisor meet one-on-one with PhD students, and what does that typically look like in a given week?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether you will have adequate mentoring access — the single most predictive structural variable for PhD success and satisfaction given that 50% of students receive under one hour per week
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If they claim frequent meetings, ask current students independently to verify — ask 'how often do you actually sit down with your advisor one-on-one?'
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If meeting frequency is low or vague, ask what the alternative feedback mechanisms are — does the lab have senior PhD students or postdocs who provide day-to-day mentorship?

diagnostic_questions.question: Has anyone in the lab or department changed advisors in the last three years, and what was that process like?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the program has functional advisor accountability and whether students have a real exit option if the relationship deteriorates — relevant given that 25% of students would change advisors retrospectively
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Ask whether the student who changed advisors was able to stay in the program and whether it delayed their degree — this reveals whether the exit option is real or theoretical
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Absence of any advisor changes in a large program may indicate either a healthy culture or a culture where students feel unable to raise concerns — probe which by asking about formal grievance mechanisms

diagnostic_questions.question: What percentage of PhD graduates from this program over the last five years are in faculty positions versus industry versus other careers?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the program's career outcomes match your goals and whether the program is honest about the academic job market's limits
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If they provide data, ask whether career support for non-academic paths is proactive or reactive — do they run industry workshops or only help students who individually ask?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If they cannot or will not provide placement data, treat that as a signal that outcomes are poor or that career support is not tracked — both are red flags

diagnostic_questions.question: Have you personally used the campus mental health services, and if so, did you find them useful?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether institutional mental health resources function in practice — given that only 26% of users found institutional support helpful, direct user experience from current students is far more informative than program descriptions
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Ask specifically what made it helpful or unhelpful — wait times, therapist familiarity with PhD-specific stress, and session limits are the most predictive variables
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Ask what they would do if they were struggling — their answer reveals what the real support infrastructure is, which is often informal peer networks rather than formal services

diagnostic_questions.question: Is there a mandatory thesis committee with annual reviews that involves faculty other than your primary advisor?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether there is structural oversight of the advisor-student relationship — programs without independent committee oversight have no mechanism to catch or correct advisor mismanagement or bullying
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Ask whether the committee is truly independent or whether advisors effectively control committee composition and whether students can raise concerns with committee members privately
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If there is no mandatory independent committee, the advisor has near-total power over the student's academic fate — this amplifies the risk of the 21% bullying rate with supervisor as perpetrator

industry_realities.common_belief: PhD student mental health struggles are primarily caused by individual resilience or adjustment issues
industry_realities.actual_reality: 39% of PhD students score in moderate-to-severe depression range compared to 6% of the general population — a 6x higher rate that is structural, not individual. The PhD environment itself is the primary causal factor.
industry_realities.implication: Prospective students should evaluate program structures and advisor behaviors as mental health risk factors, not assume their own resilience will be sufficient to offset structural problems

industry_realities.common_belief: Bullying by supervisors in PhD programs is rare or limited to a few bad actors
industry_realities.actual_reality: 21% of PhD students report being bullied, and of those, 48% identify their supervisor as the perpetrator — meaning roughly 1 in 10 PhD students is bullied by their own advisor
industry_realities.implication: Advisor vetting should include explicit investigation of supervisory behavior, not just research output — and programs should be evaluated on whether they have structural mechanisms to address supervisor misconduct

industry_realities.common_belief: High student satisfaction rates in a PhD program indicate a healthy, well-functioning environment
industry_realities.actual_reality: 75% satisfaction coexists with 36% seeking mental health help, 21% experiencing bullying, and 79% reporting career uncertainty — satisfaction reflects sunk-cost commitment and meaning-making, not absence of structural problems
industry_realities.implication: Do not use program satisfaction scores as a primary quality signal; instead probe specific structural variables: advisor access, bullying incidence, mental health outcomes, and career placement data

industry_realities.common_belief: Campus mental health services provide adequate support for PhD students who are struggling
industry_realities.actual_reality: Only 26% of PhD students who used institutional mental health support found it helpful — meaning 74% of users did not benefit from the resources their institution provided
industry_realities.implication: Prospective students should identify mental health support options outside their institution before enrolling, including private therapists covered by student insurance, and should not assume institutional availability equals functional support

industry_realities.common_belief: More than half of PhD students who want academic careers will achieve permanent academic positions within a few years of graduating
industry_realities.actual_reality: Over 50% plan academic careers but only 6% expect to become assistant professors immediately after PhD, and 46% anticipate a postdoc first — and the actual rate of permanent academic placement has been declining for decades
industry_realities.implication: Every PhD student should build non-academic career options in parallel, regardless of academic career intent — the structural mismatch between aspiration and outcomes is too large to ignore

industry_realities.common_belief: PhD programs provide adequate career guidance for both academic and non-academic paths
industry_realities.actual_reality: Only 29% of PhD students received useful non-academic career advice from their program, and 60% relied on personal research for career planning — programs systematically under-deliver on career preparation
industry_realities.implication: Career preparation must be treated as an individual responsibility requiring active external networking, not something the program will provide — students should seek industry contacts and informational interviews independently from day one

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Evaluates advisor primarily on research fit, publication record, and funding — treats the relationship as a given once intellectual alignment exists
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Treats advisor selection as a behavioral and structural vetting process — asks current and former students about mentoring style, meeting frequency, and conflict handling; checks whether the program has accountability mechanisms
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: 25% of PhD students would change advisors in retrospect — junior selection criteria miss the variables that predict whether the relationship will be functional or damaging

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Uses program ranking, satisfaction scores, and faculty prestige as primary quality proxies — accepts program-provided information at face value
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Disaggregates satisfaction data and looks at structural indicators: actual placement rates by career type, bullying incidence, advisor accountability mechanisms, and mental health resource effectiveness as reported by current users
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Surface quality signals mask structural problems that determine day-to-day experience — junior proxies produce high regret rates; senior proxies identify functional program health

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Plans exclusively for an academic career and avoids industry engagement to signal commitment — relies on the program to provide career guidance when needed
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Builds industry networks and non-academic skills in parallel with academic work regardless of career intent — recognizes that only 29% of programs provide useful non-academic career advice and acts accordingly
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Academic job market contraction means exclusive academic career planning is high-variance — students who don't build parallel options are exposed to significant downside risk with no fallback

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Assessing mental health risk before enrolling
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Treats mental health as a personal variable — assumes their own resilience will determine outcomes and takes comfort in a program listing wellness services
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Treats mental health as a structural variable determined by advisor behavior, work-hours culture, and the quality of actual (not listed) support resources — investigates these specifically before committing
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: 6x higher depression rate in PhD students versus general population is structural, not individual — treating it as personal means not vetting the environmental factors that will drive it

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Response to bullying or supervisor misconduct
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Stays silent because speaking out feels career-threatening — assumes that tolerating the situation is necessary to protect degree progress
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Identifies formal and informal escalation pathways before a problem arises — knows whether advisor-change processes exist, whether thesis committee members are accessible independently, and whether an ombudsperson is available
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Over 50% of bullied students feel unable to speak out — lack of pre-mapped pathways means students absorb the cost alone; knowing the infrastructure before it's needed changes the risk calculus
